inline: The client came to us after three years of running the homestay through OTAs. The business was doing well — the homestay was fully booked most weekends and had a 4.7 rating on Booking.com — but the owner had started to realize how much the OTA dependency was costing them.

About 90% of the homestay's bookings came through two OTAs (Booking.com and MakeMyTrip), both charging roughly 18–22% commission. On a typical weekend booking of ₹6,000 for two nights, the OTA was taking ₹1,100 to ₹1,300. Over a year, that added up to roughly ₹2,40,000 in OTA commission — a significant portion of the homestay's revenue.

Because the bookings came through OTAs, the owner did not have direct access to guest contact information. They could not send repeat-guest offers, could not build an email or WhatsApp list, and could not market directly. Every booking was a new booking, even if the guest had stayed before.

The homestay had a Google Business Profile, but no website. When potential guests searched for the homestay by name, they found the OTA listings and the Google profile, but no owned digital presence. This made the homestay look less professional than competing properties with their own websites, and it meant that all the SEO and content value went to the OTAs rather than to the homestay.

The homestay itself was strong — good rooms, good location, good reviews. The problem was not the property; it was the digital infrastructure. The owner needed a website that could take direct bookings and build a direct guest relationship, without requiring them to become a full-time marketer.

We scoped the project into four phases over seven weeks. The scope was deliberately bounded — the client wanted to launch before the Diwali season, and we agreed to postpone any work that was not essential to that goal.

inline: The scope above is the plan. This section is what the plan looked like in practice — the specific work behind the result.

The client had a mix of old photos from previous years and some smartphone photos in poor light. We hired a local photographer for a two-day shoot: every room from multiple angles, the exterior, the garden, the view from the balcony, and the breakfast spread. The photos were the single most important investment of the project — the homestay looked significantly more appealing than the previous photos suggested. The photographer cost ₹28,000, about 30% of the total project cost, and was worth every rupee.

The site was built on WordPress with a premium homestay theme, adapted to the owner's brand (which was minimal — a color palette and a logo). The structure was: home, 4 room pages, gallery, location, reviews, about, contact, and booking. Each room page had 3–5 photos, a description, and pricing (starting rates). The gallery had 30+ photos organized by category (rooms, exterior, surroundings, breakfast). The location page had a map, directions from Mumbai and Pune, and nearby attractions.

We integrated a hospitality booking platform (a common Indian provider) that handles real-time availability, rate management, and payment processing. The platform also syncs with Booking.com and MakeMyTrip, so that a direct booking on the website is reflected in the OTA calendars, and vice versa. This was the most complex part of the build, and the most valuable — it meant the owner did not have to manage two separate calendars.

We optimized the Google Business Profile (photos, hours, categories, a link to the new website) and added LocalBusiness schema to the site. We also added location-specific content — the location page mentions Diveagar, nearby attractions, and how to get there from Mumbai and Pune. This was not a heavy SEO campaign; it was the basics, done correctly.

A WhatsApp button was added to every page, especially prominent on mobile. This was the primary contact channel for most guests, and having it available on every page made a measurable difference in the inquiry volume.

The owner did not have technical experience, so we spent a training session walking through: how to update rates and availability, how to add a new photo, how to respond to a Google review, and how to use the booking platform dashboard. We also gave a written documentation guide with screenshots. This training was the difference between the site being maintained and being abandoned.
The numbers below are from the client's booking platform and Google Analytics, measured against the discovery baseline. They represent the first 90 days post-launch.

The direct booking share increased from 10% to 40% — meaning roughly 4 in 10 bookings now come through the website instead of an OTA. This is the most important result, because it directly affects the owner's margins. On ₹1,87,000 in direct bookings, the owner saved approximately ₹35,000 in commission in the first 90 days — the equivalent of roughly 8–10 weekend bookings that would have gone to an OTA.

The increase in Google reviews (from 34 to 52) was partly a side effect of more direct guests (who are more likely to leave a review when asked directly) and partly a deliberate strategy — the owner started asking every direct guest for a Google review at checkout.

blocks.text: What the numbers do not claim

inline: We did not run an A/B test — the homestay did not have enough traffic to split between two versions of the site. The direct booking increase is therefore attributed to the project, but not isolated from other factors (seasonality, marketing changes, the Diwali season). This is the honest position: the numbers are real, the attribution is reasonable, but it is not the same as a controlled experiment. If you are evaluating any case study, look for this kind of honesty about what the numbers do and do not show.

Also worth noting: the 40% direct booking share was measured during a peak season (Diwali, November–December). The share may be lower in the off-season, when OTA discovery matters more. The owner's long-term goal is 30% direct year-round, which is a more realistic target than the peak-season 40%.
The client approved the following quote for publication. We have left it as-is, including the parts that are not purely positive.

"The website changed the way we run the homestay. Before, I was paying 20% to Booking.com for every guest and never knowing who they were. Now, I know every direct guest by name, I can send them a WhatsApp message when the off-season starts, and I'm keeping the commission. The photos made a big difference — we look much better online than we did before. The only thing I'd say is that I wish I had learned the booking platform faster. It took me about two weeks to really get comfortable with updating rates and availability. The training was good, but it's more than you think at first."
— Owner, Diveagar homestay

The owner's note about the learning curve is worth emphasizing: booking platforms have a real learning curve, and the first two weeks are the hardest. We now build in two training sessions instead of one — a session at launch and a follow-up session after the owner has used the platform for a week. This is one of the changes we made after this project.
Every case study that describes only success is a marketing document, not a case study. Here is what actually went sideways.

blocks.text: The photography ran a week over

inline: We planned two days for photography, but the weather did not cooperate — one day was cloudy and the exterior photos came out flat. The photographer came back the following week to re-shoot the exterior and the views. The photos were much better for it, but the schedule slipped by a week, which compressed the website build phase. We absorbed the slip because we had a one-week buffer built into the timeline, but it was tighter than we wanted.

blocks.text: The OTA sync had a two-day setup issue

inline: The booking platform's OTA sync had a two-day setup issue — the MakeMyTrip integration required an extra approval step that we had not anticipated. During those two days, the site was live but the OTA calendars were not synced, which meant a risk of double bookings. We took the site's booking engine offline for 48 hours (guests could still book via WhatsApp) until the sync was confirmed. No double bookings occurred, but the launch was not as smooth as we had planned.

blocks.text: The initial training was too compressed

inline: The launch training was one 90-minute session covering rates, availability, content updates, review responses, and the booking platform. The owner absorbed the basics but did not fully retain everything, which showed up in the first two weeks when they struggled to update weekend rates. We added a follow-up session after week one, which helped significantly. This is now standard practice on our tourism projects.

blocks.text: What this means for your own project

inline: If a developer tells you their case study had no surprises, they are either very lucky or not telling you the whole story. Every build has surprises. The right question is not "did anything go wrong" but "how did the team handle it when things went wrong" — which is the question our
is built around.
The lessons below are the ones that generalize to any tourism website. They are not specific to this homestay.

The single biggest contributor to the direct booking increase was the photography. The homestay looked significantly better in the new photos than in the old ones, and the photos are what convince a guest to book. If you are a tourism business with mediocre photos, a photography investment will often have a bigger impact than a website redesign.

blocks.text: OTA sync is worth the complexity

inline: The OTA sync was the most complex part of the build, and the most valuable. Without it, the owner would have had to manage two separate calendars — which is error-prone and often leads to double bookings. If you are on OTAs and building a direct booking channel, budget for the OTA sync integration from the start.

The owner needed more training than we initially planned. A tourism business owner is not a web developer, and the booking platform has a learning curve. Plan for two training sessions: one at launch, one after the owner has used the platform for a week. This is much more effective than a single long session.

This project finished on schedule because we had a one-week buffer that absorbed the photography delay. Projects without buffers absorb the same delays at the launch date, which is the worst possible time to be fixing issues. Build a buffer into your own schedule, or ask your developer how they handle overruns.

The 40% direct booking share was measured during peak season, with the website fully launched. In the off-season, the share is likely lower — OTA discovery matters more when there are fewer last-minute bookings. The long-term goal is 30% direct year-round, and the owner understands that this will build over time. If you are building a direct booking channel, expect it to grow slowly — not overnight.

sections.title: How to Verify This Case Study

inline: We wrote this page so it can be checked, not just read. Here is how to verify the claims above.

The live website is publicly accessible. You can run PageSpeed Insights on it, open it on your own phone, and go through the booking flow (without completing the booking). If the performance or booking flow claims are exaggerated, you will be able to tell.
The client has agreed to speak with prospective clients. If you are considering hiring us, ask for the reference and call them. The reference can confirm the timeline, the scope, and the results.

blocks.text: Ask for the case study methodology

inline: If you are evaluating this case study against another developer's case study, ask both to explain their methodology — what was measured, how it was measured, and what the limitations are. A developer who cannot explain their methodology is a developer who does not actually measure results.

The question to ask any developer whose case study you are reading is: "What didn't go to plan on this project?" If the answer is "nothing," the case study is marketing. If the answer is specific — like the three items in the previous section — the case study is credible. For the full comparison framework, see

faqs.q: How much did this tourism website cost?
a: The total build cost was ₹95,000, including the website, booking engine integration with OTA sync, and photography. The booking platform subscription is ₹4,500 per month, and monthly maintenance is ₹3,500. The total first-year cost is roughly ₹1,60,000.

faqs.q: How long did it take to build?
a: Seven weeks from kickoff to launch. This included two weeks for photography, three weeks for the website build, one week for QA, and one week for launch and training. We also had a one-week buffer that absorbed a photography delay.

faqs.q: Why did you recommend a booking engine instead of a booking form?
a: The homestay had 4 rooms and a steady volume of bookings, and the owner wanted to reduce OTA dependency. A booking form would have been cheaper but would have required manual confirmation for every booking and would not have provided real-time availability. The booking engine was the right fit for the volume and the goal.

faqs.q: What was the hardest part of the project?
a: The OTA sync integration was the most technically complex part, and it caused a two-day delay during setup. The training was the second hardest part — the owner needed more time to learn the booking platform than we had initially planned.

The photography delay due to weather. We had planned two days for photography, but a cloudy day forced a reshoot the following week. It was handled by the buffer, but it compressed the build phase more than we wanted.

faqs.q: How long until the site paid for itself?
a: Under six months. The site generated ₹1,87,000 in direct bookings in the first 90 days, saving roughly ₹35,000 in OTA commission. At that rate, the ₹95,000 build cost would be recovered in about six months — possibly faster during the peak season.

faqs.q: Can this work for a smaller homestay?
a: Yes, with a smaller scope. A 2-room homestay might not need a full booking engine — a booking form (via WhatsApp) is often sufficient for the volume. The photography investment is still worth it, and the local SEO setup is still worth it. The scope shrinks, but the strategy is the same.

faqs.q: Can this work for other types of tourism businesses?
a: Yes, with modifications. The same approach — a website with photography, booking functionality, and local SEO — applies to guesthouses, resorts, restaurants, and activity providers. The specific booking flow and photography needs vary by business type, but the strategy is the same.

faqs.q: How does this compare to a full ecommerce build?
a: A tourism website is a different type of project from an ecommerce website. An ecommerce site is designed to sell products; a tourism site is designed to capture bookings for a stay or experience. The booking flow is simpler than an ecommerce checkout, but the photography and reviews are more important. See
